newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine, G7 outline plan for Chernobyl sarcophagus.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine, G7 outline plan for Chernobyl sarcophagus.

text.p: Ukraine and its Western partners seeking the safe closure of Chernobyl nuclear power plant outlined plans on Thursday to stabilise the crumbling sarcophagus built around the fourth reactor after it blew up 11 years ago.
Ukraine wants the sarcophagus, feared to be leaking radiation through cracks in its concrete walls, to be stabilised as part of moves to close the plant by 2000.
The two sides have held months of talks on how exactly to go about safely stabilising the enclosure.

A multi-million dollar project running through to the year 2005 has been deemed cost-efficient and effective by the Group of Seven (G7) countries' representatives meeting on the problem, Carol Kessler, head of a G7 expert group, said.
"The project may cost as much as $780 million," Kessler told a news conference with Ukraine's Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko.
Ukrainian officials and G7 experts held talks in Slavutych this week, a small town which is home to about 5,000 workers who operate Chernobyl's sole working reactor.
The fourth reactor blew up on April 26, 1986, spewing radiation across much of Europe -- though 80 percent of the pollution hit neighbouring Belarus.
The fate of the sarcophagus is the key to shutting Chernobyl, officials say.
"The first efforts will be to focus on ensuring the existing structure cannot collapse," Kessler said.

The project included stabilising the structure's walls, building shields over fuel deposits still in the sarcophagus until they can be safely removed, and building some sort of shelter over it, she said.
The G7 would put together a pledge of financial support for the project at its summit in Denver in June.
"We will also ask for other international donors to assist in financing this project on a grant basis," Kessler said.
"We hope that with the resources of the G7, other international donors and Ukraine that we can begin this project in 1997."
Ukraine estimates 4,300 people have died because of the disaster, the world's worst nuclear accident.
